chunks.title: The problem
headingPath: Sorting support tickets and escalating urgent customers before a human opens the inbox.
chunks.text: In many growing service businesses, every customer enquiry lands in one shared inbox or form sheet. A team member has to open each message, figure out whether it is a billing mistake, a technical bug, or a simple password question, check the company’s help docs, and copy the right person in Slack. That manual sorting breaks down as volume grows. Routine questions eat up the morning, while an upset customer facing an urgent billing or access failure can sit unread at the bottom of the queue for hours.

chunks.title: The result
headingPath: Sorting support tickets and escalating urgent customers before a human opens the inbox.
chunks.text: Instead of starting the day with an unsorted pile of messages, the support team opens Slack to find tickets already grouped by department, urgent issues flagged at the top, and a policy-backed draft waiting on each one. First response times drop, handoffs stay consistent regardless of who is on shift, and no upset customer gets lost behind routine admin.

chunks.title: What we did
headingPath: Sorting support tickets and escalating urgent customers before a human opens the inbox.
chunks.text: We looked at what a senior support lead actually does during the first two minutes with a new ticket, then automated that exact preparation step while keeping a human in control of the final reply. When a customer submits the support form, the workflow reads the message and assigns three clear labels: the department it belongs to (billing, technical, account, or general), the customer’s tone, and the urgency level. At the same time, the system searches the company’s approved FAQ documents and prepares a draft response based on those policies. Next, a routing rule decides where the ticket goes. Standard tickets land in their matching Slack channel with the customer’s message, classification tags, and the suggested reply ready for a teammate to review. If a ticket comes in with both negative sentiment and high urgency, the workflow bypasses the normal queue and posts straight to an urgent escalation channel so the team can step in right away. Every ticket and draft is also recorded in Airtable for tracking.

chunks.title: Details
headingPath: When to connect your existing tools instead of rebuilding
chunks.text: Replacing core business software sounds tempting when staff spend Friday afternoons exporting CSV spreadsheets, fixing broken column names, and re-uploading lists between tools. Rewriting the whole stack from scratch feels tidy on a whiteboard. Ripping out platforms that your finance desk, warehouse crew, or sales team already knows brings months of retraining, data migration bugs, and operational slowdown. When individual tools do their main job well and fail mostly at talking to each other, a dedicated integration layer delivers relief much sooner. Staff stay inside the interfaces they already understand while background services carry validated updates between systems automatically.

chunks.title: Signs an integration fits better than a rebuild
headingPath: When to connect your existing tools instead of rebuilding
Signs an integration fits better than a rebuild
chunks.text: An integration makes immediate sense when one database already holds your trusted records, such as a billing tool that sends compliant invoices or a storefront that tracks inventory accurately. Often errors only creep in afterward because someone copied numbers by hand or missed a cancelled item in another tab. When the only missing piece is an exception queue or an approval dashboard, building a focused bridge beats throwing away years of working data. Our order processing automation architecture shows that pattern clearly. Incoming web forms, staff review sheets, and dispatch alerts stay familiar to the team, while server-side validation and clean API sync move every confirmed line item without duplicate typing. Keep the tools your staff already trust; build the clean bridge where copy-and-paste errors happen today.

chunks.title: What solid integration engineering requires
headingPath: When to connect your existing tools instead of rebuilding
chunks.text: Quick no-code connections often break silently whenever a field name changes or a third-party webhook fires twice in one second. Production integrations need explicit engineering safeguards at every boundary: Idempotency keys so duplicate webhooks never generate double invoices or repeat records. Strict schema checks to catch renamed or missing payload fields before corrupt data reaches storage. Explicit network timeouts paired with retry queues for flaky third-party APIs. Clear team alerts whenever an authentication token expires or a manual override is needed. That engineering discipline keeps automated workflows dependable month after month. If a legacy vendor blocks your business completely behind closed exports or hard account limits, custom software earns its keep. Otherwise, keeping proven tools intact while building the bridge between them lowers risk and puts time back into your week sooner. Review our software and integration options or send a project brief listing the tools you want wired together.

headingPath: Stopping double-sold stock and manual payment checks for a custom bouquet shop.
chunks.text: Taking orders in chat meant answering the same price questions all day, checking GCash screenshots by eye, and risking selling a one-of-a-kind bouquet twice.

chunks.text: Online storefront, payment automation, and AI shop assistant

chunks.title: The problem
headingPath: Stopping double-sold stock and manual payment checks for a custom bouquet shop.
chunks.text: Janelle’s Satin Bouquet makes handcrafted satin arrangements in Dasmariñas, Cavite. Because every order ran through Facebook and Messenger, the owner spent hours each day replying to the same questions about prices, ribbon colors, and delivery dates before an order was even placed. Once a customer decided to buy, the manual work grew harder. Each arrangement was handmade in small batches, so two buyers messaging at the same time could claim the same bouquet before the owner updated the page. Payment checks were also done by hand: buyers sent GCash screenshots in chat, and the owner had to check reference numbers and amounts on her phone between making bouquets.

chunks.title: The result
headingPath: Stopping double-sold stock and manual payment checks for a custom bouquet shop.
chunks.text: The shop now runs live at shop.janelle-bouquet.workers.dev with a catalog, custom bouquet builder, order tracking, and a mobile admin panel. Buyers get instant answers on pricing and availability at any hour without waiting for a manual chat reply. Most importantly, the payment workflow protects the business by default. Verified payments move straight into production, uncertain claims pause safely for human review, and the owner can manage stock and orders from her phone in minutes instead of spending her evenings sorting through chat threads.

chunks.title: What we did
headingPath: Stopping double-sold stock and manual payment checks for a custom bouquet shop.
chunks.text: During diagnosis, we traced where the owner lost the most time: quoting custom bouquets, holding stock during checkout, and verifying GCash payments. Instead of handing her a complicated back-office tool meant for a warehouse team, we built a storefront and admin designed to run entirely from a phone. Customers can now browse ready-made designs, price a build-your-own bouquet step by step, or submit a custom request. When a buyer checks out, the shop holds that item immediately and generates a unique expected payment amount for GCash QR checkout. To remove manual receipt checking, we connected an automated payment matcher. When a payment text arrives, the system checks the reference number and exact amount against open orders. Clear matches confirm the order automatically. If a reference number looks reused or the amount does not line up, the system holds the order in a review queue and sends a Telegram message to the owner so she can approve or reject it with one tap. Finally, we added a shop assistant connected directly to the live product catalog.

chunks.title: Problem Brief
headingPath: Replacing manual stock checks and spreadsheet copy-paste on incoming retail orders.
chunks.text: Every new order required a staff member to check stock in a spreadsheet, calculate the total, log the row, email the buyer, and message the owner by hand.

chunks.title: Solution type
headingPath: Replacing manual stock checks and spreadsheet copy-paste on incoming retail orders.
chunks.text: End-to-end order validation, inventory routing, and notifications

chunks.title: The problem
headingPath: Replacing manual stock checks and spreadsheet copy-paste on incoming retail orders.
chunks.text: Many small retailers start by taking orders through an online form and tracking inventory in Google Sheets. The tools are familiar, but the glue between them is usually a person. For every order that arrived, someone had to check whether the customer filled in a valid email and quantity, look up the product price, check if enough units were on the shelf, copy the order into a master sheet, subtract the stock count, email the customer a confirmation, and notify the owner. When ten orders arrive at once, mistakes slip through. A typo in a spreadsheet formula or a missed stock update means a customer gets promised an item that is already sold out.

chunks.title: The result
headingPath: Replacing manual stock checks and spreadsheet copy-paste on incoming retail orders.
chunks.text: Routine orders now go from form submission to customer confirmation without anyone copying a single cell across spreadsheets. Stock counts stay accurate as orders arrive, out-of-stock requests are caught at the door, and staff only step in when an order genuinely needs human attention.

chunks.title: What we did
headingPath: Replacing manual stock checks and spreadsheet copy-paste on incoming retail orders.
chunks.text: We kept the tools the team already knew, Google Forms, Google Sheets, Gmail, and Telegram, and built an automated fulfillment pipeline to handle every handoff between them. As soon as an order is submitted, the first gate cleans and checks the details. If a submission is missing an email address or asks for an invalid quantity, the pipeline stops it right there and sends a Telegram alert to the team instead of letting bad data into the order book. Valid orders get a unique order number and check the live product sheet for current pricing and stock. An inventory router then splits the flow: When stock is available: The system calculates the order total, records the order and line items, subtracts the purchased quantity from available stock, emails a formatted confirmation receipt to the customer, and pings the owner on Telegram. When stock is short: The system logs the request to a backorder tab and alerts the owner immediately so they can contact the buyer before payment or packing begins.

chunks.title: 1. Entity status and scope
chunks.text: This Privacy Policy and Cookie Notice ("Policy") explains how Clarteon ("we", "us", "our") collects, uses, stores, discloses, and protects information when you visit this website, submit a project brief, schedule a discovery call, or interact with Clara, our automated AI assistant. Clarteon currently operates as an unincorporated founding technology team based in the Republic of the Philippines prior to formal corporate registration. Contact and data privacy inquiries may be directed to our designated point of contact at info@clarteon.tech. Where applicable, our handling of personal data is structured with reference to the principles of transparency, legitimate purpose, and proportionality under the Data Privacy Act of 2012 of the Republic of the Philippines (Republic Act No. 10173) and its Implementing Rules and Regulations.

chunks.title: 3. Cookie notice and preference management
chunks.text: This website implements a layered cookie model restricted to Strictly Essential mechanisms and optional Visitor Preference storage. We do not deploy advertising pixels, cross-site tracking cookies, or third-party behavioral profiling scripts.

chunks.title: 4. Third-party infrastructure and data transfers
chunks.text: To deliver website functionality without operating custom mail, database, calendar, or model-hosting servers, Clarteon relies on specialized third-party subprocessors, each of which may process data on infrastructure located outside the Republic of the Philippines: Vercel: Web application hosting, content delivery, and serverless request execution. Neon: Managed PostgreSQL database hosting for project briefs, booking records, anonymized question logs, and site configuration. Resend: Transactional email delivery for project brief receipts, team alerts, and booking confirmations. Google (Google Calendar & Google Meet): Automated calendar availability checks, event creation, and meeting invitations when a visitor books a call. Cloudflare (Turnstile & Web Analytics): Bot mitigation and cookieless aggregate performance measurement. Groq: Real-time text inference and transient speech-to-text transcription for Clara. Each provider processes only the minimum data required to perform its technical function and acts subject to its own security controls and published privacy terms.

chunks.title: 5. Data retention and minimization
chunks.text: Project briefs: Retained in our lead database for up to twelve (12) months from submission, after which records are scheduled for deletion or anonymization unless an ongoing engagement or statutory obligation requires continued retention. Discovery-call bookings: Retained only for as long as reasonably necessary to coordinate, conduct, and follow up on the scheduled meeting, unless superseded by a written client contract or legal retention requirement. Anonymized unanswered chat logs: Retained strictly for documentation maintenance without personal identifiers. We practice data minimization in application logs by excluding full form bodies, personal emails, and chat payloads from routine server diagnostics.

chunks.title: 6. Children and minors
chunks.text: This website and its inquiry, booking, and AI chat services are intended strictly for business and adult use. Individuals under eighteen (18) years of age must not submit personal information, schedule calls, or use Clara. If we become aware that personal data of a minor has been submitted inadvertently, we will delete it promptly upon notice.

chunks.title: 7. Your rights and requests
chunks.text: Subject to applicable law and technical feasibility, you may request access to, correction of, or deletion of personal information you have submitted through our project brief or discovery-call forms, or withdraw consent to future non-essential processing. To submit a privacy, access, or deletion request, email info@clarteon.tech from the email address associated with your submission or include sufficient information to locate your record. A member of our team will respond directly.

chunks.title: 8. Amendments to this policy
chunks.text: We may update this Policy from time to time to reflect technical changes, new service providers, or updates after incorporation and formal counsel review. The current effective date appears at the top of this page.

chunks.title: 9. Legal review notice
chunks.text: This document is prepared in good faith as a transparent, operational policy reflecting Clarteon's actual website behavior prior to incorporation. It is subject to final review and formal approval by a qualified lawyer admitted to practice in the Republic of the Philippines and does not constitute legal advice.

chunks.title: a. Strictly essential cookies and security tokens
headingPath: a. Strictly essential cookies and security tokens
chunks.text: Strictly essential storage is necessary for website security, session continuity, fraud prevention, and honoring your stated consent preference. These mechanisms operate automatically upon use of the relevant feature and cannot be disabled without impairing site functionality: clarteoncookieconsent: Stores your saved cookie consent selection (essential or all) for one hundred eighty (180) days (SameSite=Lax, path /). clarteonchat: Signed HttpOnly session cookie scoped strictly to /api/chat (SameSite=Lax) used to maintain conversation context during an active browser visit and enforce fair-use message quotas. clarteonadmin: Signed HttpOnly session cookie (SameSite=Lax) set exclusively when an authorized team administrator signs into the protected /admin portal. Visitors who do not sign in as administrators never receive this cookie. Cloudflare Turnstile tokens: Ephemeral human-verification challenges executed when initializing chat, submitting project briefs, or booking calls to mitigate automated spam and abuse.

chunks.title: The problem
headingPath: Checking suspicious texts and screenshots for scams without sending private messages to the cloud.
chunks.text: Scam messages in the Philippines closely mimic GCash, Maya, local banks, parcel couriers, job offers, and even messages from relatives. When someone receives an urgent text asking them to click a link or confirm a code, they want a quick, reliable second opinion. The catch is privacy. The very messages people need to check often contain one-time passwords, account balances, or personal family conversations. Uploading those screenshots to a cloud chatbot puts sensitive data on someone else’s server, and most international tools misread Tagalog and Taglish phrasing or stop working without mobile data.

chunks.title: The result
headingPath: Checking suspicious texts and screenshots for scams without sending private messages to the cloud.
chunks.text: Sane is live at sane-ph.vercel.app as an installable web app that works offline after the first visit. Across the project’s evaluation sets, it identified 15 out of 15 scam messages in the primary test set and 16 out of 16 in the secondary set without flagging legitimate bank or personal messages as scams. For businesses handling sensitive client records, medical notes, or financial documents, Sane demonstrates how our team builds practical AI tools where private data stays on the device by design.

chunks.title: What we did
headingPath: Checking suspicious texts and screenshots for scams without sending private messages to the cloud.
chunks.text: Built with team What If I Call for the AppBuildersPH 2026 Local AI challenge, we designed Sane around a strict constraint: the app had to work without a backend server so a user’s message could never leave their phone. Instead of relying on a single AI model that might guess, we layered three checks inside the browser: Rule checks for known traps: Instant checks flag lookalike bank domains, shortened links, and pressure tactics asking for PINs, OTPs, or advance fees. Pattern matching across languages: A compact language model running directly on the device compares the message against common scam scripts in English, Filipino, and Taglish, plus a screenshot reader that extracts text from images. Plain-language explanations: When a device supports on-device AI acceleration, a local model explains why the message was flagged in everyday terms without overriding the safety verdict.

chunks.title: Author Role
headingPath: Stop buying software before you map the bottleneck
chunks.text: Chief Executive Officer (CEO)

chunks.title: Details
headingPath: Stop buying software before you map the bottleneck
chunks.text: Most businesses do not run into trouble because they lack software. A growing team usually already pays for a CRM, group chat apps, shared spreadsheets, an invoicing tool, and folders of exported reports. When delivery slows down or leads slip away, buying one more platform feels like the fastest way out. Weeks later, staff still copy numbers from one browser tab into another because the new platform covered the tidy ten percent of the job and left the messy middle untouched. When we talk with operators during a discovery call, we ask them to walk through the last order, ticket, or client inquiry that went sideways. Almost every delay sits between existing tools. Someone caught an email on a phone, pasted details into a group chat, updated a spreadsheet at the end of a shift, and forgot to tell billing when a detail changed. Putting a fresh interface on top of that sequence adds one more inbox for someone to forget to check. Software only saves hours when it removes a handoff your team actually drops today.

chunks.title: Follow one piece of work from arrival to close
headingPath: Stop buying software before you map the bottleneck
Follow one piece of work from arrival to close
chunks.text: Before you commit budget to custom development or automation, three questions clear out guesswork: Where does your team type the same detail more than once in an ordinary week? Which handoff stalls the moment one key person steps out for the afternoon? How do staff notice when something goes off script, such as a missing file or a changed delivery window? Answering those questions takes an hour with the people handling daily work. Out of twenty annoying chores in a department, two usually account for most wasted time and client frustration. One company needs order rows moved straight from web forms into invoicing and fulfillment queues, as shown in our manual order processing workflow architecture. Another team loses warm inquiries simply because nobody answers off-hours questions or offers an open calendar slot right away.

headingPath: Stop buying software before you map the bottleneck
What to ask any technical partner to deliver
chunks.text: When you hire a technology partner, you pay to remove operational friction. Ask to see the exact state of a request before the build begins and how it changes after launch. A serious deliverable list spells out which manual steps go away, how the system behaves when an external API hiccups briefly, and how your own staff monitor issues without calling a developer for every routine adjustment. If you are weighing workflow automation, a tailored web portal, or an integration between tools you already own, browse our operations solutions or book a discovery call to map your slowest handoff together.

chunks.title: The problem
headingPath: An AI business coach that cites clinic records and operating policies instead of guessing.
chunks.text: Aesthetic clinic owners track rebooking rates, treatment conversions, and lapsed clients in their database, while their consultation scripts and staff policies live in uploaded documents. When a clinic manager asks a practical question like “Why is CoolSculpting down this month, and what does our consultation handbook say we should change?”, a standard AI chatbot cannot help. It has no access to the clinic’s real numbers and will happily invent a policy that sounds plausible. For V-Unite’s clinic coaching challenge, the goal was to build an assistant that clinic owners could talk to by voice or text between appointments and trust enough to act on.

chunks.title: The result
headingPath: An AI business coach that cites clinic records and operating policies instead of guessing.
chunks.text: The system runs live at v-unite-voice-ai-coach.vercel.app and is protected by 88 automated quality checks. One of those checks specifically tests what happens when an owner asks about a policy the clinic has never uploaded: the assistant states plainly that no matching document exists instead of making up an answer. Each coaching conversation ends by saving a short session summary and a concrete action plan, turning scattered clinic data and static PDFs into a daily decision tool.

chunks.title: What we did
headingPath: An AI business coach that cites clinic records and operating policies instead of guessing.
chunks.text: We started from the rule that an operational assistant is only useful if the owner can see where every answer came from. We designed a clean coaching workspace paired with an automation workflow that decides what evidence a question needs before generating a word of advice. When an owner asks about sales, retention, or lapsed clients, the assistant queries the clinic’s customer records and KPI calculators directly. When the question is about staff procedures or pricing rules, it searches the clinic’s uploaded SOP documents. When a question touches both, it pulls the numbers and the matching handbook section together so the recommendation connects what is happening in the data to what staff are supposed to do at the front desk. Because clinic managers often check in between appointments, we added push-to-talk voice alongside text chat. Spoken questions go through the exact same verification steps as typed ones, and the assistant speaks back a concise summary while showing the cited records on screen.

chunks.title: Details
headingPath: What a clear software scope includes before work starts
chunks.text: Many founders sign a build proposal after scanning a neat list of page names or feature headlines. Short labels such as "custom admin dashboard" or "automated booking flow" look straightforward at kickoff. Delays start midway through the build when both sides realize they pictured different workflows for cancellations, staff approvals, timezone shifts, or missing client details. Those surprises turn a focused build into rounds of rework. A dependable technology partner settles the unglamorous questions while changes only cost a paragraph of text. Before engineering begins, a written scope should show how real visitors, customers, and staff move through every state of the system, including moments when a connection drops or an input fails checks. Changes cost almost nothing in a written paragraph; they cost weeks once three integrations depend on the old assumption.

chunks.title: Four pieces every delivery plan needs
headingPath: What a clear software scope includes before work starts
Four pieces every delivery plan needs
chunks.text: When you review a scope from Clarteon or any other build team, check that it spells out concrete behaviors you can test on a preview link: Input validation and recovery rules: How every form, checkout, and scheduler handles invalid fields, accidental double clicks, slow connections, and third-party downtime. Database-first persistence: Guaranteeing records save locally before emails or calendar invites fire, so a temporary provider blip never drops a lead silently. Operator visibility: Giving staff one clean workspace to inspect incoming records, update statuses, retry failed notices, or edit published copy without touching code. Testable acceptance checks: Closing each milestone with actions you can click through yourself, from mobile screen behavior to real confirmation receipts. We follow this discipline whether shipping a storefront such as Janelle's Satin Bouquet or wiring internal scheduling rules. Short milestones keep working software visible early, while adjustments stay inexpensive.

chunks.text: Detailed scope notes protect both the buyer and the engineers building the system. Listing edge cases up front separates must-have first-release functionality from nice ideas worth saving until customers use the product. Teams spend less energy sending clarification emails and more time reviewing live working previews. chunks.text: Before approving a chatbot or workflow agent for your company, ask how the build team verifies edge cases before go-live. chunks.title: Details
headingPath: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where plain rules win
chunks.text: Businesses bring two opposite worries to AI conversations. Some teams ask a language model to run an entire multi-step process without supervision, while others steer clear completely after watching a public chatbot invent policies or guess availability. Both reactions come from treating language models as an all-or-nothing substitute for ordinary software engineering. Language models read messy human messages well. They summarize customer complaints, pick requested dates or SKU details out of cluttered email threads, and route questions toward the right documented answer. Standard server code handles arithmetic, database permissions, live calendar checks, and state updates identically every time. Dependable AI systems keep those two responsibilities sharply divided. Let language models interpret messy human intent; keep arithmetic, calendar rules, and database writes inside deterministic server code.

chunks.title: Give rules the strict checks and let models read intent
headingPath: Where AI agents earn their keep, and where plain rules win
Give rules the strict checks and let models read intent
chunks.text: Look at customer triage or spoken practice feedback, similar to the workflows behind our customer support triager architecture and V-Unite voice AI coach. When a visitor writes a broad question in plain English, the model searches curated knowledge entries and explains the relevant service or process. When that same visitor picks a meeting time or leaves contact details, deterministic server tools query live availability, enforce schema validation, check anti-spam tokens, and write verified records to the database. Even inside chat interactions, clear technical guardrails keep replies trustworthy: Ground every factual claim in reviewed knowledge documents, with an honest handoff whenever a detail is missing. Keep pricing, custom quotes, legal commitments, and deadlines strictly in human hands. Route every database write or staff notification through typed tool validation and rate limits.

chunks.title: Details
headingPath: Why clunky intake forms and slow booking pages quietly lose leads
chunks.text: A prospect opens your website on a phone between meetings, reads two sections, and decides to get in touch. What happens over the next minute shapes whether that inquiry lands in your pipeline. When layout blocks jump around during load, mobile menus collide, or the only option is an email address with no response expectation, busy buyers close the tab and move to the next search result. Fast, intentional web engineering fixes an acquisition leak long before a sales call takes place. Effective websites skip noisy popups and countdown banners in favor of clear explanations, fast page transitions on mobile connections, and immediate paths for qualified visitors to book a time or submit structured context. Most lost leads never leave angry feedback; they simply close a frustrating mobile form and never come back.

chunks.title: Small interface failures that add up
headingPath: Why clunky intake forms and slow booking pages quietly lose leads
Small interface failures that add up
chunks.text: During website reviews, the same friction points appear across service firms and growing shops: Booking widgets that force manual timezone math or trap visitors in multi-day email ping-pong before a calendar link arrives. Long intake forms demanding twelve mandatory fields upfront, alongside unguided boxes that force staff to chase basic details afterward. Mobile layout shifts, broken tap targets, and silent network errors on cellular connections right when someone hits Submit. Case studies buried in stale downloadable PDFs instead of readable, scannable web pages. When we shipped the ordering flow for Janelle's Satin Bouquet and the local-first interface for Sane, keeping primary actions clear on every viewport width stayed front and center. On Clarteon's own website, visitors can inspect past systems and check real open discovery slots in their local timezone without leaving the page.
